description: Between 1347 and 1353, bubonic plague killed 30 to 60% of Europeans. A health catastrophe that shook medieval society and sped up the shift into a new world.

hero.hook: In six years, Europe lost up to half its population.

blocks.text: Between **1347** and **1353**, Europe was struck by the **Black Death**. Caused by the bacterium **Yersinia pestis**, it killed between **30 and 60%** of the population, some **25 to 50 million** people.

Europeans were already weakened by the famines of the [[Little Ice Age]], a cooling of the climate that ruined harvest after harvest. The plague was more than a health crisis. It was an accelerator of history: it shook the feudal order and forced society to rebuild itself on other terms.

The bacterium first circulated among the rodents of Central Asia. The [[Pax Mongolica]], a spell of relative peace under the Mongol Empire, and the [[Silk Road]], the trade network linking Asia to Europe, offered it safe routes west. At the Genoese trading post of [[Caffa]] in Crimea, besieged by the [[Golden Horde]], a Mongol empire of the steppes, the disease tipped into the Mediterranean. Galleys fled toward Italy.

blocks.caption: Plague burials: Europe discovers mass death

blocks.text: In **October 1347**, they docked at **Messina**, in Sicily. The ships were driven out again, but the sickness was already ashore. In **1348** it reached Marseille, then the whole of Europe along the networks of the Italian merchants.
The siege of Caffa is often cited as one of the first examples of biological warfare: the Mongols are said to have catapulted infected corpses over the walls.

Doctors relied on [[Galen]], a Greek physician of antiquity, and on [[Miasma theory]]: the idea that disease came from corrupted air. They never saw the real carrier, the rat flea ([[Xenopsylla cheopis]]). When the rats died, the fleas moved on to people.

blocks.caption: The plague doctor and his beaked mask: protection more symbolic than effective

blocks.text: The bubonic form swelled the lymph nodes. The septicemic form blackened the skin. The pneumonic form passed straight from person to person and killed in **24 to 48 hours**. In crowded, filthy towns it spread at terrifying speed.

Society buckled. The [[Flagellants]] whipped themselves in public to appease God. Art invented the Dance of Death. With no explanation to hand, people looked for culprits: the [[Jewish pogroms (1348-1349)]] bloodied the Rhone valley and the Holy Roman Empire. Accused of poisoning wells, thousands of Jews were massacred. Pope [[Clement VI]], then in Avignon, tried to protect them. Too little, too late.
In Avignon, Clement VI stayed between two large fires to “purify the air.” The heat kept the fleas at a distance, and he survived.
[[Boccaccio]], the Florentine writer, described fathers abandoning their own sons. Charity, neighborliness, family: everything cracked under the fear of contagion.

events.title: Retreat

blocks.text: Around **1353**, the pandemic receded. Labor had become scarce. Wages rose, feudal dues fell, and serfdom retreated across Western Europe. Lords now had to negotiate. The catastrophe had, paradoxically, strengthened the survivors.

The failure of the authorities in the face of the plague also fed a critical spirit. People observed more and doubted the old dogmas. By emptying villages and reshuffling inheritances, the Black Death prepared, in spite of itself, the ground for the Renaissance.
Between **1347** and **1353**, the Black Death killed up to half of Europe. That demographic shock weakened the feudal order, pushed up the price of labor and hurried the arrival of a new world.
